rv.q: Ingram’s Nina is an unfussy, recognizable creation — an unshakable heroine worthy of her eponym, in a play whose revival reminds us of its writer’s ability to put a spell on us.
Adding to the play’s power is Ms. Morisseau’s unflinching lack of sentimentality.
Whether or not they always come together into fully compelling pieces of theater is another question.
Ingram in particular, under director Steve H. Broadnax III’s elegant direction, makes you believe revolution is only a matter of time.
Sunset Baby is one of those dramas that has appreciated with age, shining with intensity in the twilight of America’s postwar order.
This production puts Sunset Baby where it belongs, next to her best works.
She doesn’t mar her record here.
If the set-up feels overwhelming, overwrought, what unfolds is slow-moving and too often muddled.
Ingram is sensational as Nina, a woman still mourning the death of her mother, a heroic figure who succumbed to drugs in the end, even as she struggles to put her own life in order.

cn.t: Morisseau's drama about revolution's legacy receives a potent, electrifying revival led by Moses Ingram. Critics praise its trenchant exploration of trust and history, though some find its construction middle-of-the-road.
